key_insight: Not all errors in proxy rewards are equally harmful: some classes of reward imperfections can actually steer policy-gradient optimization toward better behavior, so evaluation should distinguish beneficial from harmful deviations rather than treating all mistakes as bad.
problem_solved: Addresses the gap in how proxy rewards for RL-trained language models are evaluated — showing that standard metrics (e.g., ranking accuracy) can be misleading because they treat all reward errors as uniformly negative and miss when imperfect rewards still guide learning in desirable ways.
method: Theoretical analysis of policy-gradient dynamics to characterize which model outputs gain probability mass under different kinds of reward misspecification.
Formal categorization of imperfect rewards into classes (e.g., harmless, harmful, and beneficial errors) based on their effect on optimization trajectories.
Derive evaluation criteria and practical guidelines that go beyond ranking accuracy to assess whether a proxy reward will help or hinder policy-gradient training.
impact: Provides practitioners a finer-grained framework for designing and selecting proxy rewards in RL for language models, enabling safer and more effective RLHF by recognizing when imperfect signals can still be useful.
visual_elements: Taxonomy diagram showing categories of reward errors (beneficial / harmless / harmful) with short examples for each.
Flow diagram of policy-gradient optimization illustrating how different reward types attract probability to different outputs.
Side-by-side chart comparing traditional metrics (ranking accuracy) vs. proposed evaluation criteria on hypothetical reward perturbations.
Guideline flowchart for practitioners: assess reward class → predict optimization effect → decide to use/refine reward.
paper_title: When Errors Can Be Beneficial: A Categorization of Imperfect Rewards for Policy Gradient
paper_authors: Shuning Shang, Hubert Strauss, Stanley Wei, Sanjeev Arora, Noam Razin
